publication.basis: the date of the publisher's post that announces the tool

entries.applicability: Stated for the Akira ransomware the post describes: the 64-bit and 32-bit Windows builds, and files encrypted by the Linux build when the Windows decryptor runs under WINE. The post says a native Linux decryptor was in development when it was written. It does not say whether builds reported after its date are covered.

prerequisites.text: One unencrypted file and its Akira-encrypted counterpart; the tool uses the pair to find the password. A larger pair is better, because the size limit follows Akira's block-size calculation.
The password-cracking step usually takes seconds but needs a lot of memory; the post strongly recommends the 64-bit build. Running as administrator is recommended.

limitations: The size of the file pair can set a limit on the size of the files that can be decrypted.
It does not decrypt files of an unrelated, older ransomware also called Akira that the post says was discovered in 2017.
Success depends on following the publisher's instructions, above all on choosing a suitable file pair.

publication.basis: the date of the publisher's post that announces the public release

entries.applicability: The post names no Rhysida versions; it distinguishes 32-bit and 64-bit encryptor samples only.

prerequisites.text: Run the decryptor, and its password-cracking step, on the PC where the files were encrypted; do not copy files from other machines to the PC that decrypts.
The default assumes a 64-bit encryptor; a command-line parameter switches to 32-bit. A testing mode checks whether decryption will work without changing files.
The cracking step needs a large amount of memory.

limitations: Results can depend on the drive letter set, the file order, the number of CPU cores, the bitness of the encryptor and the original file format.
Common formats (Office documents, archives, pictures, multimedia) are covered; files in less common or proprietary formats are not unless the publisher adds support.
Small text files (source code, INI, XML, HTML and similar) must be above a minimum size to be decrypted.

publication.basis: the date of the news report that describes the tool

entries.applicability: The report says the tool works on encryptors used from November 2022 until about a week before the report, when the developers fixed the bug it relies on; it names the period, not versions. It says older variants that append the .basta extension are not supported.

prerequisites.text: Recovery needs the plaintext of 64 encrypted bytes. For files without large runs of zero bytes, an older unencrypted copy with similar content may help.

limitations: Files under 5,000 bytes cannot be recovered; files from 5,000 bytes up to 1 GB can be recovered in full; for files over 1 GB the first 5,000 bytes are lost and the rest can be recovered.
The scripts work on one file at a time.
Encryptors after the fix the report mentions are not covered by the technique.
